8. Romania's capital, Bucharest, once wanted to be...Ferris.
Around a hundred years ago, people called it Little Paris, grand boulevards, French-style palaces, cafes, everywhere.
And then Bucharest went one step further. It built its own Arc de Triomphe.
The first one was made of wood in 1878, just so the army could march under it after independence.
Today's stone arch was finished in 1936, and it's 27 meters tall.
Paris has the original, Bucharest has the copy.
But copying Paris is normal.
Number 7 is a cemetery that tells jokes.
7. The Mary Cemetery in the village of Sapunza
In 1935, a local artist named Stan Ewan Patrasche carved a wooden cross for a grave and painted it bright blue.
Then, he added a painting of the person's life and a short poem about them.
And the poems are funny. Some of them roast the person who died. Some of them roast their mother-in-law.
Today, there are more than 800 of these crosses, a cemetery where people go to laugh, which
is a pretty Romanian way to deal with death.

Number five is a road.
Number five, the Transfagarasan.
In 1968, the Soviet Union invaded Czechoslovakia,
and Romania's leader, Nicolai Ceausescu, got nervous.
What if the Soviets came for Romania next?
His army needed a fast way across the Carpathian Mountains.
So, from 1970, they blasted a road straight over them,
hairpin after hairpin, up to 2,042 meters.
The invasion never came, but the road is still there,
And in 2009, Top Gear called it the best road in the world.
One catch, snow closes it for most of the year,
usually from late October to late June.
And those mountains have residents
who don't care about any of this, big ones, with claws.
Number four, Romania has more brown bears
than any country in Europe outside Russia.
Scientists counted them with DNA
from more than 24,000 samples of hair and droppings.

Bears wander into towns, through streets, and straight into people's bins.

Number two, Salina Turda, a salt mine in Transylvania.
People have been digging salt here since at least 1271.
By hand, the miners carved out chambers almost 100 meters tall.
The mine closed in 1932, and then Romania did something wild with it.
It turned the bottom of the mine into a theme park, deep underground.
There's a Ferris wheel, bowling, mini golf, table tennis, and amphitheater.
And in the deepest chamber, an underground lake, where you can rent a rowing boat.
It's the only place I know where you can go bowling inside a salt shaker.

Number one, Movil Cave near the Black Sea.
